content: The measles laboratory network in the Western Pacific Region comprises 383 laboratories, including one global specialized laboratory, three regional reference laboratories (RRLs), 17 national measles laboratories (NMLs), and, in China, 31 provincial and approximately 331 prefectural laboratories. The World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for the Western Pacific accredits the RRLs, NMLs, and the 31 Chinese provincial laboratories. By March 2012, nearly all network laboratories had been accredited. This network plays a critical role in serologic testing (ELISA) for anti-measles and anti-rubella IgM antibodies and in the genetic characterization of viruses detected from cases and outbreaks. WHO accredits these laboratories based on well-established criteria. Key indicators and targets for epidemiological surveillance quality include: At least 80% of surveillance units reporting measles data to the national level on time. A reporting rate of at least two non-measles, non-rubella cases per 100,000 population at the national level. At least 80% of second administrative level units reporting at least two non-measles, non-rubella cases per 100,000 population. At least 80% of suspected cases undergoing adequate investigation. At least 80% of suspected cases having adequate specimen collection (excluding epidemiologically linked cases). At least 80% of specimens reaching the laboratory within five days of collection. At least 80% of laboratory-confirmed transmission chains (two or more confirmed measles cases) having adequate specimens for virus detection tested in an accredited laboratory. Laboratory performance indicators include: 100% of measles network laboratories being WHO-accredited for serological and virological testing. At least 80% of serological results reported within four days of specimen receipt. 100% of laboratories conducting measles diagnostic testing having adequate quality assurance mechanisms. At least 80% of virus detection and genotyping results completed within two months of specimen receipt. Population immunity should be analyzed by birth cohort, considering vaccine-induced and natural immunity since the introduction of the measles vaccine. This analysis should account for changes in routine vaccination schedules and supplementary immunization activities (SIAs). Special attention should be given to underserved and marginalized groups, such as migrants, urban or rural poor, and those in remote areas, to identify potential immunity gaps. Experience in countries like Vietnam and the Philippines suggests that high coverage among children and adolescents is critical for interrupting measles virus transmission, even if adult immunity levels are not universally high. Administrative coverage estimates, population-based surveys, and serosurveys are essential tools for assessing vaccination coverage and immunity. These data sources help identify gaps in immunity and areas requiring targeted interventions. Rapid coverage assessments following mass vaccination campaigns can provide additional insights into local-level coverage. Sustainability of national immunization programs is crucial for maintaining measles elimination. This includes ensuring resources for mass campaigns, where appropriate, and preparing costed outbreak preparedness plans. Verification of measles elimination should assess whether elimination can be sustained, highlighting strengths and weaknesses in national immunization programs and surveillance systems. This assessment should inform national action plans to address programmatic gaps and strengthen health systems. Genotyping evidence is vital for verifying the interruption of endemic measles virus transmission. The absence of previously endemic strains for over 12 months supports elimination. Genotypes D9 (Philippines, Malaysia) and H1 (China) were endemic in the Western Pacific Region in 2012, while genotypes D4 and D8 were frequently imported from Europe and South-East Asia. Virological surveillance and genetic sequencing, combined with epidemiological investigations, help differentiate endemic from imported cases and determine if endemic transmission has been re-established. The Regional Verification Commission (RVC), Subregional Verification Committee (SRVC), and National Verification Committees (NVCs) are responsible for verifying measles elimination. The RVC is the sole body authorized to verify elimination at the regional level. These committees guide countries in meeting verification criteria and compiling evidence. The RVC also contributes to global measles eradication efforts by sharing knowledge and evaluating updates to verification criteria. Documentation for verification must demonstrate that endemic measles virus transmission has been interrupted for at least 36 months under standard surveillance conditions. Countries must submit annual progress reports, regardless of their readiness for verification. These reports should include background information, epidemiological data, surveillance quality, population immunity, program sustainability, genotyping evidence, and validation by the NVC or SRVC. The RVC, SRVC, and NVCs also play advocacy roles, raising awareness and promoting commitment to measles elimination among health officials, professionals, and political leaders.
